scenario.title: Support backlog
scenario.initial_request: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

M-RESP-TIME.name: Median ticket response time vs SLA

M-IBAN-FAIL-COUNT.name: Count of refund payments failing with FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT

M-REFUND-FAIL-RESOLUTION-RATE.name: Share of FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds successfully reprocessed
M-REFUND-FAIL-RESOLUTION-RATE.denominator: total refunds currently in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status (5)

M-REFUND-TICKET-SHARE.name: Share of refund-related tickets attributable to a failed refund
M-REFUND-TICKET-SHARE.numerator: tickets linked to a FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refund

F-01.statement: Median ticket response time is 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets.

F-02.statement: Ticket volume underlying the response-time record is 900 tickets.

F-03.statement: payment-db.refund_failures returned 5 refund records, all with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT.

CL-01.statement: Build a chatbot so customers stop waiting for answers about refunds

CL-02.statement: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

H-SLOW-RESPONSE-TIME.statement: Customers wait too long for refund answers because support agents are too slow to reply to tickets, so a chatbot providing instant answers would resolve the backlog.

H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY.statement: The backlog stems from actual delays or failures in processing refund payments (DA-PAY), so customers keep contacting support because their refunds are genuinely stuck, not because answers are slow to give.

H-TOOL-MALFUNCTION.statement: An underlying tool or system failure (reflected in the scenario id C-TOOLFAIL) in ticket-db or payment-db is causing missed or delayed updates, driving repeat contacts rather than slow human replies.

H-PROCESS-BOTTLENECK.statement: The refund process (P-REF) itself has inefficient steps or handoffs causing ticket backlog, independent of response speed or payment delays, so a chatbot would not address the structural bottleneck.

H-TICKET-VOLUME-LOAD.statement: The 900-ticket volume itself, even with fast per-ticket replies, may be creating a visible backlog/queue effect unrelated to response speed or payment processing.

interpretation_history.interpretation: Ticket-db shows a median response time of 2 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets, meaning support replies are far faster than the service target, not slow. This undercuts the stakeholder's framing that customers wait on slow agent replies, while leaving the source of backlog (volume, payment delays, or process steps) unexplained.

payment-db shows 5 refund records failing with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, indicating these refunds are genuinely stuck due to payment-processing errors rather than merely delayed replies. This gives a concrete, data-based mechanism for refund-related support contacts that is independent of ticket response speed.

E-03.content: Customers wait forever; a chatbot would answer instantly.

interpretation_history.interpretation: SH-SUP restates the same speed-framing already recorded as CL-01 ("customers wait forever, chatbot answers instantly"), adding no new data; it is a repetition of the stakeholder's flagged bias ("frames everything as response speed") and does not engage with E-01 (fast replies, within SLA) or E-02 (IBAN payment failures) which already undercut that framing.

U-UNK-TICKET-LINK.question: What fraction of the 900 refund-related tickets correspond specifically to refunds stuck in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, versus other causes such as sheer ticket volume (H-TICKET-VOLUME-LOAD) or a process bottleneck (H-PROCESS-BOTTLENECK)?
U-UNK-TICKET-LINK.decision_impact: Determines whether fixing IBAN failures resolves most of the backlog or only a small, known subset, which changes the scope and expected impact of the remediation.
U-UNK-TICKET-LINK.resolution_path: Join ticket-db records with payment-db refund status to measure the share of the 900 tickets tied to a failed refund.
U-UNK-TICKET-LINK.safe_placeholder: Treat the 5 confirmed IBAN failures as the known, fixable subset; do not claim the fix resolves the full 900-ticket backlog until measured.

U-UNK-TOOL-MALFUNCTION.question: Is an underlying tool/system issue (H-TOOL-MALFUNCTION, CANDIDATE) in ticket-db or payment-db causing missed status updates that drive repeat contacts, separate from the IBAN failures themselves?
U-UNK-TOOL-MALFUNCTION.decision_impact: If a tool malfunction exists, remediation must include a system-health fix in addition to correcting IBAN data, otherwise repeat contacts could continue even after refunds are fixed.
U-UNK-TOOL-MALFUNCTION.resolution_path: Audit ticket-db and payment-db logs for missed-update incidents around the failed refunds.
U-UNK-TOOL-MALFUNCTION.safe_placeholder: Proceed with IBAN-failure remediation now, since both tools currently report HEALTHY; treat a tool-health audit as a parallel, non-blocking check.

U-UNK-VALIDITY-METRIC.question: Does the single aggregated median response time (2.0h) across 900 tickets hide a slow-responding subgroup, or is it a valid proxy for 'customers are not waiting on replies'?
U-UNK-VALIDITY-METRIC.decision_impact: If a long-tail subgroup of tickets has much slower response times, the rejection of H-SLOW-RESPONSE-TIME may not hold uniformly across all refund tickets.
U-UNK-VALIDITY-METRIC.resolution_path: Pull the full response-time distribution (not just the median) from ticket-db for refund-related tickets.
U-UNK-VALIDITY-METRIC.safe_placeholder: Use the committed median-based SLA compliance (E-01) as the current best evidence while flagging distribution analysis as pending.

A-TICKET-REFUND-LINK.statement: At least part of the 900-ticket volume consists of customers following up on refunds stuck in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT, even though no direct join between ticket-db and payment-db records has been evidenced.

A-IBAN-FAILURE-ONGOING.statement: The 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records observed in payment-db reflect an active, ongoing processing issue rather than an already-resolved historical snapshot.

SC-ROOTCAUSE.statement: Root cause of refund-related ticket contacts is correctly attributed to payment-processing failures (IBAN format errors) rather than slow agent response time.
SC-ROOTCAUSE.validation_method: Review the committed payment-db refund_failures records (E-02) and ticket-db response-time stats (E-01).

SC-RESOLVE-KNOWN.statement: All currently known FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds are corrected and reprocessed.
SC-RESOLVE-KNOWN.validation_method: Re-query payment-db.refund_failures after remediation and confirm zero remaining FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT entries.

SC-BACKLOG-REDUCTION.statement: Refund-related repeat-contact tickets tied to stuck refunds decrease after remediation.
SC-BACKLOG-REDUCTION.threshold: measurable decrease; exact target pending UNK-TICKET-LINK
SC-BACKLOG-REDUCTION.validation_method: Compare refund-linked ticket volume before and after remediation using a ticket-db/payment-db join.

VOB-U-UNK-TICKET-LINK.reason_deferred: deferred at DEFINE Gate; safe placeholder: Treat the 5 confirmed IBAN failures as the known, fixable subset; do not claim the fix resolves the full 900-ticket backlog until measured.
VOB-U-UNK-TICKET-LINK.validation_method: Join ticket-db records with payment-db refund status to measure the share of the 900 tickets tied to a failed refund.

VOB-R-2.unresolved_question: Is an underlying tool/system issue (H-TOOL-MALFUNCTION, CANDIDATE) in ticket-db or payment-db causing missed status updates that drive repeat contacts, separate from the IBAN failures themselves?
VOB-R-2.reason_deferred: proposed by reasoner R-11: H-TOOL-MALFUNCTION remains CANDIDATE with no supporting or contradicting evidence; resolving it determines whether the diagnose_iban_format_failure_cause deliverable can close U-UNK-TOOL-MALFUNCTION or must flag an unresolved systemic risk.
VOB-R-2.validation_method: Compare ticket-db and payment-db status-update timestamps/logs around the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT records for missed/delayed update patterns indicative of tool malfunction.

problem_definition.requested_solution: Build a chatbot so customers get instant answers about refund status, on the premise that slow agent replies are what makes customers wait (SH-SUP initial request, CL-01).
symptoms: Support lead reports customers waiting for answers about refunds and requests a chatbot to give instant answers (CL-01, SH-SUP initial_request).
900 refund-related tickets exist in ticket-db while payment-db shows 5 refund records stuck in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT status (E-01, E-02).
problem_definition.root_problem: Refund-related support contacts are driven by refunds that fail to process — payment-db shows 5 refund records failing with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-02) — not by slow agent replies, since ticket-db shows a median response time of 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets (E-01). Customers whose refunds are stuck in this payment-processing failure keep contacting support, which the stakeholder misreads as a 'customers wait forever for slow answers' problem (H-SLOW-RESPONSE-TIME, rejected).

structural_remedies.description: Add client-side IBAN format validation at refund submission in process P-REF to stop new FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT failures from occurring.
structural_remedies.rationale: A format/checksum check is a deterministic config change that does not require calling the DEGRADED bank-api (ticket-db and payment-db are HEALTHY).; residual gap: Does not fix the 5 already-failed records (E-02) or diagnose the OPEN U-UNK-TOOL-MALFUNCTION question about missed status updates.

structural_remedies.description: Correct the IBAN data and resubmit the 5 known FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds (DA-PAY) to satisfy SC-RESOLVE-KNOWN.
structural_remedies.rationale: Resubmission likely requires bank-api, which is DEGRADED with a NOT_TRANSIENT ACCESS_DENIED hold and no fallback path (recovery_decision, seq 63), so completion cannot be guaranteed under current tool health.; residual gap: Until bank-api access is restored or an alternate settlement channel is authorized, the 5 stuck refunds (and any new ones) cannot be fully reprocessed.

structural_remedies.description: Introduce a deterministic linking key (e.g., refund reference) between ticket-db and payment-db so refund-linked tickets can be identified going forward, closing U-UNK-TICKET-LINK.
structural_remedies.rationale: Both source systems are HEALTHY and this is a schema/process change within ORG-1's own data assets (DA-PAY, DA-TCK), not dependent on bank-api.; residual gap: A-TICKET-REFUND-LINK notes no direct join currently exists; retroactively attributing the historical 900 tickets still requires content-level matching that a schema change alone cannot provide.

structural_remedies.description: Define explicit ownership and an escalation path within P-REF for refund payment failures (IBAN errors) so they are routed to a payments owner rather than surfacing only as support tickets.
structural_remedies.rationale: P-REF currently has no actors/steps/systems recorded; assigning ownership is a governance/process definition, not a tool-dependent action.; residual gap: Addresses recurrence prevention but does not retroactively reduce the existing 900-ticket backlog or confirm SC-BACKLOG-REDUCTION.

decision_log.rationale: causal chain: Refund requests are submitted with invalid IBAN formatting and fail payment processing (E-02: 5 payment-db records with status FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT). → These refunds remain stuck, unresolved, in payment-db with no automatic recovery (E-02). → Customers whose refunds are stuck follow up with support, contributing to the open refund-related ticket volume (inferential link, see assumption ticket_refund_link). → Support agents reply quickly (median 2.0 hours vs a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets, E-01), so the backlog customers experience is not caused by slow replies but by the unresolved payment failure behind the contact.; rejected framings: [('H-SLOW-RESPONSE-TIME', "Contradicted by E-01 (median reply time 2.0h, well within the 24h SLA) and by E-02 (concrete payment-processing failures); it only restates the stakeholder's initial request/bias (SH-SUP 'frames everything as response speed', E-03/CL-01/CL-02) and is the requested solution's premise, not an evidenced cause.")]

actions.question: What do agent/ticket response-time metrics in ticket-db show for refund-related tickets over the backlog period?
actions.expected_information_gain: Reveals whether agent reply latency is actually elevated, directly testing CL-01's 'slow_response_time' claim and the chatbot premise.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: If response times are not elevated, the stated justification for a chatbot (H-SLOW-RESPONSE-TIME) collapses and the next decision shifts toward investigating payment/process causes instead.
actions.why_now: This is the one catalog item whose operation name (response_times) directly names the exact mechanism H-SLOW-RESPONSE-TIME claims, so it is the highest-value first check.

actions.question: Does payment-db show elevated refund processing failures or stuck/delayed refund transactions during the backlog window?
actions.expected_information_gain: Shows whether refunds are genuinely stuck in payment processing, which would support H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY and undercut the chatbot's instant-answer rationale.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: A spike in refund_failures would redirect the fix from chatbot/response-speed toward payment-pipeline remediation, a materially different intervention.
actions.why_now: refund_failures is the catalog item that most directly names the mechanism H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY describes (DA-PAY stuck refunds), so it should be checked now against this live hypothesis.

actions.question: Does bank-api settlement status indicate external settlement delays independent of the retailer's own refund-processing steps?
actions.expected_information_gain: Would clarify whether a payment delay (if found) originates externally at the bank rather than internally, refining H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: Only matters as a follow-up refinement of H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY and bank-api is not listed in scenario.tool_surface, so access/authority is uncertain.
actions.why_now: bank-api is absent from the declared tool_surface (only ticket-db and payment-db are listed), so this query carries authority/access risk and should only run as a secondary check after payment-db:refund_failures.

actions.question: Beyond response speed, what specific steps or handoffs in the refund process does the support lead describe as causing delays?
actions.expected_information_gain: May surface process-step or handoff inefficiencies in P-REF that no tool query covers, informing H-PROCESS-BOTTLENECK.
actions.decision_impact_rationale: No tool-query catalog item describes process steps/handoffs directly, so this interview is the only remaining avenue to test H-PROCESS-BOTTLENECK, though SH-SUP's noted bias toward framing issues as response speed limits its discriminative power.
actions.why_now: H-PROCESS-BOTTLENECK remains live and no TOOL_QUERY item names process/handoff mechanics, so the interview is the most direct remaining catalog item for it despite the stakeholder's known bias.

proposal.summary: The initial request was to build a chatbot because customers wait too long for refund answers (CL-01, SH-SUP), but evidence contradicted this framing: ticket-db shows replies average 2.0 hours against a 24-hour SLA across 900 tickets (E-01), while payment-db shows 5 refunds stuck in FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT (E-02). The problem definition (PD-1) therefore attributes refund-related support contacts to payment-processing (IBAN) failures rather than slow responses, with H-SLOW-RESPONSE-TIME rejected and H-PAYMENT-PROCESSING-DELAY supported. The DEFINE gate passed conditionally, deferring the question of how much of the 900-ticket backlog is actually tied to these failures (VOB-U-UNK-TICKET-LINK). What was released is a diagnostic deliverable (W-WI-01-IBAN-DIAGNOSIS) confirming the 5 FAILED_IBAN_FORMAT refunds as the attributable root cause, within the scope diagnose_iban_format_failure_cause:DA-PAY. The release decision is RELEASE_WITH_KNOWN_LIMITATION: automated verification passed its structural checks but failed a semantic consistency check, because a proposed remedy (reprocessing the known failed refunds) is marked feasible yet is also documented as blocked by the bank-api tool being DEGRADED (a non-transient access failure led to a HOLD on bank-api). No release-blocking hold was triggered, but several open verification obligations, unknowns, and unimplemented remedies are explicitly carried forward as known limitations rather than resolved.
